title: Jam & Preserves
strapline: Squashy fruit, a bubbling pot and a jar to label — catching summer in a spoonful.
intent: Making jam shows children a dramatic transformation — soft fruit and sugar becoming a thick, glossy, spreadable preserve — and lets them wonder at how heat changes food.
Mashing, stirring and spooning are satisfying hand skills, and washing and hulling fruit is careful, purposeful work.
Filling, labelling and dating jars gives mark-making and early writing a genuine job, and the row of finished jars is a proud, visible result.
Preserving connects children to the seasons and to the idea of keeping food for later — a real, useful piece of understanding the world.
Jam made from fruit children helped pick or grow closes a memorable loop from bush to breakfast.
Every culture preserves its harvest, so the activity can welcome chutneys, pickles and jams from the families in the room.
implementation: Let children wash and mash the fruit themselves — a potato masher and a bowl of strawberries is joyful, purposeful work.
Do the hot boiling as the adult's job, but keep children watching and narrating: 'it was runny, look how thick it's getting'.
Make labels together — the fruit, the date, a drawing — and stick one proudly on every jar.
Talk about why we preserve: 'the strawberries are only here in summer, but this jar keeps them for winter'.
Pick or buy the fruit with the children first so they know exactly where the jam began.
Spread the finished jam on the bakery's bread at snack, and send a jar home with families who cooked.
key_questions: It was runny — look how thick it's getting. Why do you think that is?
Why do we make jam to keep the strawberries?
What shall we write on the label — the fruit, the date, a drawing?
How does the fruit change when it's mashed and boiled?
Where did our jam begin — do you remember picking the fruit?

impact.text: Children watch a dramatic transformation — soft fruit and sugar becoming a glossy preserve.
Children wash, hull, mash and stir — careful, purposeful hand skills.
Children fill, label and date jars, giving mark-making and early writing a genuine job.
Children connect to the seasons and the idea of keeping food for later.
Children meet the preserves of many families — chutneys, pickles and jams.

enhancements: Picking or buying the fruit with the children first so they know where the jam began.
Labels made together — the fruit, the date, a drawing — for every jar.
The finished jam spread on the bakery's bread at snack.
A jar sent home with each family who cooked.
Family recipes for chutneys and pickles shared alongside the jam.

playing_exploring: Mashing ripe fruit is a gloriously squashy, sensory job, and children test how thoroughly they can crush it.
Children handle real fruit and watch a genuine, vivid change happen in the pot.
active_learning: Filling and labelling a whole row of jars is absorbing, careful work, and children take real pride in the finished shelf.
creating_thinking: Children grasp a real idea — that cooking and jarring can keep summer fruit for the cold months — and connect it to the seasons they know.
